title: The End of PCOS: Why the Biggest Name Change in Women's Health Hits South Asian Families Hardest
excerpt: A 14-year global effort has rebranded polycystic ovary syndrome as PMOS — a shift that could transform how millions of Indian women and NRIs are screened for diabetes and metabolic disease.
body:
For millions of South Asian women, a diagnosis of polycystic ovary syndrome has long meant a narrow conversation — irregular periods, trouble conceiving, perhaps a referral to a gynaecologist. The condition's very name steered both patients and physicians toward the ovaries, even as mounting evidence showed that the real damage was metabolic: insulin resistance, creeping weight gain, and a sharply elevated risk of Type 2 diabetes that shadowed women for decades after their reproductive years ended.

That era of mislabelling is now formally over. On 12 May, a global consortium of 56 patient and professional organisations — publishing in *The Lancet* and presenting at the European Congress of Endocrinology in Prague — announced that PCOS would henceforth be known as Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome, or PMOS. The single-letter swap from C to M may look modest on paper, but it represents a 14-year effort to reframe a condition that the World Health Organisation estimates affects one in eight women of reproductive age worldwide, with 70 per cent of cases going undiagnosed.

## Why the old name failed

The "polycystic" in PCOS referred to a pattern of small follicles visible on ultrasound — but these are not cysts, and many women with the condition never develop them. The misnomer had real clinical consequences. "Doctors would focus on the cystic presentation," explained Rachel Morman, chair of Verity, a UK advocacy group. "Patients could be dismissed if they didn't present with cysts, even as they suffered from the metabolic and fertility issues linked with the condition." Patients, too, would attribute unrelated ovarian cysts to PCOS, missing opportunities for timely diagnosis of other conditions.

Professor Helena Teede of Monash University, who led the renaming effort, said the old terminology "reduced a complex, long-term hormonal disorder to a misunderstanding about cysts and a focus on ovaries." The new name, chosen by 87 of 90 voting consortium members in a "landslide," foregrounds the endocrine system and metabolic disruption that define the disorder.

## South Asian women bear a disproportionate burden

The rename matters everywhere, but nowhere more acutely than for women of South Asian descent. Research published in *Diabetes Care* found that South Asian women in the United States have a 2.6-fold higher odds of PCOS compared to Chinese and Filipina women, alongside a 1.7-fold higher risk of diabetes. In India, prevalence estimates range from 7.2 per cent under conservative NIH criteria to nearly 20 per cent using the broader Rotterdam definition — with a study in Delhi NCR finding that 17.4 per cent of young women screened positive.

The reasons are partly genetic. Endocrinologists describe a "thin-fat phenotype" common among South Asians: even at normal body weight, higher levels of visceral fat and lower muscle mass produce hidden insulin resistance. Modern urban lifestyles — sedentary work, refined carbohydrates, chronic stress, disrupted sleep — amplify the metabolic risk. For many Indian women, health takes a backseat to familial and professional obligations, delaying the very screening that could prevent a slide from PMOS into full-blown diabetes.

## What NRIs should know

For the estimated four million Indian women in the US alone, the rebrand carries practical implications. A global survey of ethnic Indian women with PCOS found an average one-year delay between first symptoms and seeking care, with women living outside India reporting lower satisfaction with dietary and lifestyle advice from their physicians.

The PMOS label should make it easier for NRI women to advocate for comprehensive metabolic screening — fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipid panels — rather than the ovary-focused ultrasounds that have historically dominated consultations. It also provides a framework for family conversations in communities where reproductive health remains culturally sensitive. The consortium deliberately avoided the word "reproductive" in the new name, partly because "in many cultures and world regions, it was felt to be too stigmatising and likely to cause harm," said Teede.

The transition will not happen overnight. Medical coding systems, patient education materials, and insurance classifications will need updating over a three-year window, with full implementation expected in the 2028 international guideline update. But the directional shift is clear: a condition that was once filed under gynaecology is now staking its claim in endocrinology and metabolic medicine, where the evidence always said it belonged.

For South Asian families navigating a genetic predisposition to insulin resistance, the message is straightforward: PMOS is not merely about fertility. It is a lifelong metabolic condition that demands early detection, regular screening, and sustained lifestyle management — and finally, a name that says so.
